orientation-independent representations can be learned using two learning principles: minimizing reconstruction error and maximizing representational inertia.

how the brain transforms the egocentric representations of space that are provided by the senses into the orientation-independent representations that are stored in the hippocampus.
how the mammalian brain learns orientation-invariant representations from egocentric sensory input and how these representations are transformed into egocentric coordinates for motor output.
how orientation-invariant representations of space may be learned and stored in the brain, as a prerequisite for spatial learning and memory.

these results demonstrate that a combination of the two learning rules can lead to orientation-invariance.

the proposed learning principles provide a framework for the development of orientation-invariant representations of space in neural networks, and thus may provide a mechanism for learning allocentric-to-egocentric transformations in the mammalian hippocampi.

the proposed learning principles can account for the formation of orientation-invariant representations in neural circuits, and thus may be a key mechanism for learning the allocentric-egocentric transformation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we present two different learning algorithms that are able to transform egocentic sensory representations into orientation-independent, allocentric ones, and vice versa.

the brain learns egocentric-allocentric transformations by minimizing reconstruction error and maximizing representational temporal inertia, and this is a principle that can be implemented in neural networks.

the learning principles of minimization of reconstruction and maximization of temporal inertia are sufficient to explain how the brain can learn orientation-independent, long-term representations of space.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a simple learning rule, which we term the principle of temporal inertia, can be used by neural circuits to learn orientation-invariant representations of space, which can in turn be used to learn long-term memory representations.
orientation-invariance can be learned through a combination of reconstruction error minimization and maximization of temporal inertia in the representations.

orientation-invariant spatial representations are not necessarily learned through an explicit transformation process, but can instead be learned by a simple minimization of the error between sensory inputs and internal neural representations.
